content: The World Health Organization (WHO) will provide technical assistance to its Member States to support the implementation of the Housing and Health Guidelines (HHGL) in a manner tailored to each country’s specific priorities and needs. This will involve collaboration across all levels of the organization and with other United Nations agencies involved in housing-related activities. A modular toolkit is currently being developed to facilitate the implementation of these guidelines at the country level. This toolkit will include resources to assist with priority setting, needs assessment, stakeholder mapping, policy analysis, intersectoral dialogue, and outreach and advocacy efforts. The implementation teams will be interdisciplinary, and the toolkit will include knowledge translation products such as policy briefs and training materials to foster intersectoral collaboration and mutual understanding. The Health in All Policies approach emphasizes that health ministries must act as stewards in other sectors to ensure that health objectives are integrated into their policies. This includes advocating for access to social housing for vulnerable groups, ensuring housing standards, and empowering vulnerable populations to improve their security and ownership. Many health ministries have not fully engaged with the health impacts of housing, often because housing is considered the responsibility of other government departments. Implementing the HHGL requires different responsibilities for authorities, property owners, and occupants, depending on the administrative and legal frameworks of each Member State. In some countries, housing responsibilities are distributed across multiple government departments, including housing, construction, energy, urban planning, transport, public health, finance, industry, and the environment. Policies in other sectors, such as immigration, wages, workforce training, and tax policy, also influence housing supply and affordability. The HHGL highlights the interconnections between housing and health, serving as a foundation for health ministries to collaborate with other ministries to improve national and local housing standards. Effective policy coordination between government departments is essential for implementing the HHGL. This may involve advocating for healthy housing, communicating potential health risks and benefits, and participating in housing assessments and building codes. The health sector can ensure that housing interventions avoid harm and improve health and safety, while also identifying individuals and households that would benefit most from such interventions. Implementing the HHGL offers an opportunity to strengthen the health sector’s engagement with communities, creating a platform for primary environmental action and fostering collaboration among governmental organizations, non-governmental organizations, communities, households, businesses, and individuals. This approach can support strategic planning, active monitoring, and social control in decision-making processes related to healthy housing strategies. Health advocates should be represented in decision-making forums concerning construction and planning. WHO will work with health ministries to ensure that health perspectives are strongly represented in housing-related policies. The implementation toolkit will include training materials to promote intersectoral dialogue and prioritize healthy housing on the agendas of policymakers within and outside the health sector. The HHGL draws on systematic reviews of research assessing the impact of specific exposures or interventions on health outcomes. While multifactorial interventions cannot attribute specific health effects to individual components, they can improve a range of health outcomes. For example, the Healthy Housing Programme in South Auckland, New Zealand, addressed multiple health risks by improving insulation, ventilation, and reducing crowding, leading to significant reductions in acute hospitalizations. Similarly, the Breathe-Easy Homes in Seattle, USA, reduced exposure to asthma triggers through moisture-reduction features, enhanced ventilation, and low-emission materials, resulting in fewer asthma symptoms and urgent clinical visits. Upgraded housing for slum dwellers in El Salvador, Mexico, and Uruguay improved living conditions by addressing housing risk factors such as dampness, pests, and flooding. This intervention led to increased satisfaction with housing quality, improved child health, and enhanced cognitive development. Multifactorial approaches, which address multiple risk factors simultaneously, are efficient and cost-effective, reducing costs while improving health outcomes. Policymakers should consider the co-benefits of such interventions when enacting regulations or subsidizing home modifications. Economic analyses demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of housing interventions. For example, lead removal and retrofitting insulation have shown significant health benefits relative to their costs. The New Zealand insulation subsidy program yielded a benefit-to-cost ratio of nearly 4:1, with even higher ratios for children and older adults. Home safety modifications to prevent falls have also been found to be cost-effective, with benefits outweighing costs by 6:1 in some cases. Improvements in water and sanitation access have similarly demonstrated high returns on investment, particularly in developing regions. Training is essential for implementing the HHGL. Health professionals require evidence-based training and technical assistance to target communities in substandard housing and address hazards. Housing sector professionals, including housing agencies, need specialized training to identify and remediate housing problems and construct better housing. Cross-sector collaboration between health and housing professionals should be encouraged, and the health and safety of workers involved in housing construction and remediation must be prioritized. WHO and its partners will provide hands-on guidance, technical assistance, and training to drive positive changes in health and housing policy and practice at all levels. The HHGL recommendations will be disseminated through a broad network of international partners, including WHO offices, health ministries, building and construction ministries, WHO collaborating centers, and other United Nations agencies.
